source: សៀវភៅស្ដីពីដំណាំដំឡូងមី (Book on Cassava), Part 2, UNDP-supported capacity-building programme for cassava, March 2015, Sections 9.2-9.3
text:
The source describes Cambodia's phytosanitary inspection procedure for cassava exports, administered by the Plant Protection, Sanitary and Phytosanitary Department (PPSPD) under the General Directorate of Agriculture (GDA), in line with the WTO SPS Agreement, in five steps:

Step 1 - Submit inspection request: the exporter submits a phytosanitary inspection request (PQI) to PPSPD at least 10 days before the planned shipping date.
Step 2 - Inspection: a PQI inspector examines the goods for hygiene and phytosanitary compliance and takes samples according to protocol.
Step 3 - Laboratory testing: where inspectors observe signs of pest infestation or contamination, samples are sent for laboratory confirmation.
Step 4 - (Certificate issuance, based on inspection/lab results.)
Step 5 - Non-conformance handling: goods found not to meet requirements may be subject to treatment, rejection, or destruction, following relevant policy; the source notes a roughly 6-hour window is allowed for urgent treatment/handling before shipment in some cases.

For exports to China specifically, the source lists a set of regulated quarantine pests/weed seeds that Chinese authorities screen for in cassava chip shipments, including: Lasioderma serricorne (cigarette beetle), Pharaxonotha kirschii, Sitophilus granarius, Sinoxylon spp. (non-Chinese populations), Oryzaephilus surinamensis, Trogoderma granarium (khapra beetle), Heterobostrychus aequalis, Prostephanus truncatus (larger grain borer), and the weed seed Cenchrus echinatus.

The source also describes a company registration requirement for exporting cassava chip/pellet to China: exporting factories/companies must be inspected and approved by Cambodia's Ministry of Agriculture (GDA) and related agencies for quarantine and hygiene compliance, and must appear on a list recognized by China's AQSIQ (General Administration of Quality Supervision, Inspection and Quarantine) before they are permitted to export to the Chinese market.
caveat: This is new, directly actionable export-compliance content not previously in the knowledge base. Step 4 of the five-step inspection procedure was not fully legible in the source image and is described only in general terms (certificate issuance) rather than verbatim; the roughly 6-hour handling window mentioned under Step 5 should be treated as approximate.
